svg.title: Threat model of full disk encryption
svg.desc: A hand-drawn systems sketch of a full disk encryption design: a boot chain running from firmware through a boot manager to an OS loader, a platform security processor holding a sealed volume key released to an encrypted volume, a recovery key escrowed to a cloud account, and the device's own sign-in looping back into that same account. Five device states are shown along the bottom with the volume key marked present or absent in memory for each. Four weak points are marked: an unauthenticated bus between the boot manager and the security processor, a signed but obsolete boot component satisfying the sealing policy, the volume key resident in DRAM while the device sleeps, and the loop where the device signs into the same account holding its recovery key.

g.text: A key held by a chip, released at boot, escrowed to the account the device signs into.

svg.text: Bus probing on the PSP channel, cold boot and DMA against a sleeping machine,
exposed ports. Buys cost, needs possession. It does not scale.

Users will not retain it, so it is escrowed
Ciphertext is malleable, tampering goes undetected
Holds the recovery key after provisioning

Single point of failure: close it, lose the key

svg.text: the states a device is actually in, left to right through its working life
Gold arrows are flows the design still governs.
Red-brown arrows mark where that control runs out, including a loop back to the
1. Unauthenticated bus: on a discrete part, the PSP's channel is readable in the clear.
2. Signed but obsolete: sealing to a signing authority admits a genuine, outdated component.
3. Key in DRAM while asleep: the state a device is actually in when it is stolen.
4. The escrow loop: the device signs into the very account holding its own recovery key.
